# Bayh–Dole, Reagan, and Valley Ideology {#sec-4-10}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1980–1990
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a regional elite capture national policy?

**The answer.** By supplying the personnel and the argument. Reagan's economics
came substantially from an institution on Stanford's campus, and the Bayh-Dole
Act of the same year let universities patent federally funded research. One
statute turned public money into private licensing revenue, and one think tank
turned a regional politics into a national one.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, now written
into statute, and elite network reproduction operating at the level of national
policy. This is the chapter where the Hoover Institution's function, planted in
Act II ch. 5, finally pays off.

**The key fact.** Bayh-Dole allowed universities to take title to inventions
made with federal research funding. The public pays for the research; the
university patents the result; the licensee monopolises it. Act II ch. 11's
triangle acquired an intellectual property regime.

**The human anchor.** George Shultz and Milton Friedman, both at the Hoover
Institution, both routed into national power — the archive Hoover built in 1919
functioning exactly as an archive of power should.

**Excluded voices.** The taxpayer, whose research funding became private
licensing revenue without a corresponding return, and the industries and regions
that Reagan-era policy did not favour. Also the biotech patients on the
receiving end of the pricing that Genentech's model made possible.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that a regional elite captured national policy by
showing its economic programme, its personnel, and its institutional base all
originate in one corridor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

The Bayh-Dole Act of 1980 is the least famous consequential statute in this
book. It allowed universities to take title to inventions made with federal
research funding, which means the public pays for the research, the university
patents the result, and a licensee monopolises it. Act II's university-
contractor-state triangle acquired an intellectual property regime, and the
technology licensing office became a standard feature of American higher
education.

Stanford's case is concrete. The Cohen-Boyer recombinant DNA patents, developed
with federal funding and licensed broadly, generated hundreds of millions of
dollars in royalties. Public research, private royalty stream, and an
institution whose incentives had just been permanently realigned toward
commercialisation.

The same year, Reagan's election brought California conservatism to Washington,
and a substantial part of its intellectual apparatus came from the Hoover
Institution — Milton Friedman, George Shultz, and a pipeline of personnel into
the administration. The archive Herbert Hoover began assembling in 1919, in Act
III chapter 5, was now functioning exactly as an archive of power is supposed to
function, and the chapter names the payoff explicitly.

Capital gains reductions and deregulation followed, and venture capital grew
sharply across the early 1980s. Genentech's 1980 initial public offering,
resting on the Cohen-Boyer work, established that biology could be financed like
software and that life itself could be an asset class.

Valley ideology assembles here: meritocratic self-description, deregulatory
politics, and continued dependence on federal funding, held together without
apparent strain. The chapter describes the contradiction accurately and without
sneering, because most of the people holding it hold it sincerely.

The taxpayer's return on the research is the chapter's excluded party, along
with patients on the receiving end of the pricing that the new model permitted.

The pipeline now runs to Washington in both directions. Act IV's inauguration
platform is visible from here.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Beats

1. **Hook.** A statute nobody has heard of that changed what a university is.
   Open on Bayh-Dole, not on Reagan.
2. **What Bayh-Dole did.** Title to federally funded inventions. The mechanics
   of technology licensing offices that follow.
3. **Stanford's licensing revenue.** Concrete: the Cohen-Boyer patents, and what
   they earned. Public research, private royalty stream.
4. **The Hoover Institution in 1980.** Friedman, Shultz, and the pipeline into
   the administration. Then look back at Act II ch. 5 and name the payoff
   explicitly.
5. **Capital gains and deregulation.** What changed and who benefited. Venture
   capital's growth across the early 1980s, sourced.
6. **Genentech's 1980 IPO.** Biology as an asset class. Recombinant DNA out of a
   Bay Area laboratory into a public offering; the Cohen-Boyer patent underneath
   it.
7. **Valley ideology assembled.** Meritocratic self-description plus
   deregulatory politics plus federal funding retained. Name the contradiction
   without sneering at it; it is held sincerely by most of the people holding
   it.
8. **The excluded.** Taxpayer return; drug pricing; regions outside the favoured
   corridor.
9. **Landing.** The pipeline now runs to Washington in both directions. Act IV's
   inauguration platform is visible from here.

::: {.chapter-question}
How does a regional elite capture national policy?
:::

The least famous consequential statute in this book is the Bayh-Dole Act of
1980.

It provided that universities, small businesses, and non-profits could take
title to inventions made with federal research funding. Before it, the position
varied by agency and the default in much of the government was that publicly
funded inventions belonged to the public. After it, the university patents the
result of research the taxpayer paid for, licenses it to a company, and collects
a royalty.

Act II chapter 11 described a triangle with an unresolved question at its
centre: who owns the output. In 1980 the question was answered, and the answer
was the university.

## What followed immediately

Every research university in the United States built a technology licensing
office. Stanford already had one — established in 1970, and among the first
anywhere — which meant it was positioned when the statute arrived.

Its most valuable asset was already in hand. The Cohen-Boyer patents on
recombinant DNA, arising from work by Stanley Cohen at Stanford and Herbert
Boyer at the University of California, San Francisco, were filed in the
mid-1970s on research funded principally by the National Institutes of Health.
Stanford licensed the technology broadly and non-exclusively at modest rates
rather than granting an exclusive licence, and it earned the universities a very
large sum over the life of the patents — a few hundred million dollars, split
between the two institutions.

The non-exclusive approach is worth marking, because it is the best version of
the arrangement. The technology was available to anyone who wanted it, an entire
industry was built on it, and the universities were paid. It is the version
defenders of Bayh-Dole point to, and they are right to.

The case against is equally structural. The public funded the research through
NIH grants, and then bought the resulting products at prices set by patent
holders. Royalties flowed to institutions rather than to the agency that paid
for the work. And the incentive created — patent everything, license exclusively
where possible — reoriented university research toward what could be owned.

## Genentech

The commercial demonstration came the same year.

Genentech had been founded in 1976 by Boyer and the venture capitalist Robert
Swanson, on the recombinant DNA technique, and it went public in October 1980.
The stock rose sharply on the first day of trading in one of the more dramatic
debuts of the era, on a company with essentially no product revenue.

What that offering established is that biology could be financed like software:
long development timelines, binary outcomes, enormous returns on the ones that
work, and a valuation resting on intellectual property rather than on cash flow.
The venture model from chapter 5 had found a second industry.

Life became an asset class in 1980, on a Stanford and UCSF patent, funded from
Sand Hill Road.

## The Hoover payoff

Ronald Reagan was elected in November 1980, and a substantial part of the
intellectual apparatus of his administration came from a building on the
Stanford campus.

The Hoover Institution had spent the decades since Act II chapter 8 assembling
what a defeated president had begun: a permanent body of scholars developing a
particular set of economic and foreign policy arguments, sustained through a
period when those arguments were entirely out of fashion.

Milton Friedman joined Hoover in 1977. George Shultz was there before becoming
Secretary of State in 1982 and returned afterwards. The Institution supplied
personnel, position papers, and intellectual standing to an administration
committed to deregulation, tax reduction, and a harder line in the Cold War.

That is what Herbert Hoover built the archive for. He founded it in 1919 to
collect the documentary record of how power moves; it became, over sixty years,
an instrument for moving it. Act II chapter 5 argued that whoever gathers the
documents acquires interpretive power. This is the interest payment.

## The capital consequences

The policy changes of the early 1980s reached the Valley directly.

Capital gains tax rates had been cut in 1978 and were cut again in 1981, which
raised the after-tax return on exactly the kind of long-horizon equity
investment that venture capital makes. Combined with the 1979 ERISA
clarification from chapter 5, the effect on the amount of capital available to
venture funds was transformative, and the industry grew by an order of magnitude
across a few years.

Deregulation in telecommunications, finance, and transportation opened markets
that technology firms would later occupy. Defence spending rose sharply, which
flowed to the corridor described in chapter 4.

## The other Californian import

The administration brought a second Californian export to Washington, and it had
been tested in the state a decade earlier.

Reagan had been governor of California from 1967 to 1975, and the politics that
carried him to Sacramento were substantially about the universities: the
Berkeley Free Speech Movement, the campus unrest described in chapter 7 of this
act, and a promise to restore order. In office he presided over the beginning of
the end of free tuition in the California public system, which had been a
founding principle of the 1960 Master Plan.

That is a durable shift and it belongs in this chapter because it inverts the
arrangement Act II described. The G.I. Bill and the Master Plan had made higher
education a public good financed collectively. From the 1970s the cost migrated
to the student, through fees and then through debt, on the argument that the
private returns to a degree were substantial and the beneficiary should pay.

The argument has force. It also converts a credential from something a society
provides into something an individual purchases, which changes who can obtain
one and what they must do afterwards to service the purchase.

Proposition 13, passed by California voters in 1978, capped property taxes and
required supermajorities for new taxes, permanently constraining the revenue
base of the state's schools and local government. It was the most influential
state ballot measure in modern American history and it was widely imitated.

So the same decade that vastly increased the flow of public research money into
a private university's patent portfolio also began withdrawing public support
from the system that had made California's technical workforce possible. Both
movements originated in California and both went national.

## The ideology, described accurately

What assembled in California in these years is a coherent position, and the
chapter's obligation is to describe it without sneering, because most of the
people holding it hold it sincerely.

It runs roughly as follows. Markets allocate better than governments. Regulation
protects incumbents and suppresses innovation. Individual technical talent is
the scarce resource and should be rewarded accordingly. The people who build
valuable things deserve what they earn, and the mechanism that identifies them
is approximately fair.

Set against that the material in this act. The semiconductor industry's early
volume came from federal procurement. The network came from a defence agency.
The research came from federal grants routed through a university, on land
granted to a railroad. The capital came substantially from pension funds
admitted by a regulatory reinterpretation. The patents on which the biotech
industry was built came from federally funded work, assigned to universities by
statute.

The contradiction is not hypocrisy, and calling it hypocrisy would be the lazy
version. It is something more interesting: a genuine belief in market
allocation, held by people whose own position was produced by an unusually large
and sustained programme of public investment, who did not experience that
investment as such because it arrived through institutions — a university, a
research contract, a pension allocation — rather than as a cheque.

Public subsidy that arrives through an institution is invisible to the person it
benefits. That is the most durable finding in this book, and Act IV is what
happens when the people it benefits acquire the government.
